etymology: The KJV “anise” translates the Greek anethon, which is properly dill, not the sweet aniseed of the confectioner. Tyndale and the Geneva Bible rendered it “anise,” and the Authorized Version kept the word.
biblical_def: In the KJV anise is a garden herb — dill (Greek anethon) — one of the small potherbs the Pharisees were careful to tithe. The modern reader hears “anise” and thinks of the licorice-flavoured seed of the confectioner’s shop; the AV means the humble dill of the kitchen garden, a plant so slight that a scrupulous man counted out its very seeds to give a tenth to God. That care was not wrong. Our Lord did not condemn the tithing of anise; He said, “these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Mat 23:23). The sin of the Pharisee was not that he tithed his dill but that, weighing out his herbs to the last seed, he “omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith.” He strained at the little and swallowed the great. The law itself had bound Israel to tithe: “Thou shalt truly tithe all the increase of thy seed, that the field bringeth forth year by year” (Deu 14:22). But the same LORD who required the tenth required first the heart: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8). Anise stands, then, for the smallest duty faithfully kept — good, but never a substitute for justice, mercy, and faith.
webster_summary: A garden herb, properly dill, tithed by the scrupulous Pharisee — not the licorice-seed of the modern shop.

Mic 6:8

corruption_summary: No postmodern quarrel here, only a botanical mistake: our “anise” is a different seed from the KJV’s dill, and the danger is the Pharisee’s, not the culture’s.
corruption_paragraphs: The confusion in this word is honest and botanical. The Greek anethon is dill; the “anise” of the modern grocer is a different plant, Pimpinella anisum, grown for its sweet licorice seed. The translators used the name that was current in their day, and a reader who pictures aniseed rather than dill loses nothing of the doctrine, for the point does not hang on the species of the herb but on its smallness. Whatever the plant, it was a trifling thing to tithe, and the Pharisee tithed it to the seed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of duties. Anise-tithing is not condemned; it is commended — “these ought ye to have done.” The error is to be exact in the little and lawless in the great: to count the seeds of dill and forget judgment, mercy, and faith. The natural heart loves this trade, because small precise duties are cheap and can be seen, while justice and mercy cost the whole man and cannot be paraded. Let the Christian tithe his anise — keep the small commandments carefully — but let him never imagine that scruple in trifles will excuse him from doing justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly with his God.
roots_summary: The word names the dill of the garden, the least of tithed herbs.

etymology: “Cummin” (also spelt cumin) comes through Latin cuminum from Greek kyminon, itself of Semitic root (Hebrew kammon). It names a slender aromatic seed-plant of the parsley kind, sown broadcast and beaten out with a rod.
biblical_def: In the KJV cummin is a small seed-spice of the garden, sown, threshed, and tithed. The modern reader may not know the plant at all, or may confuse it with the mint and dill beside it in the Pharisee’s tithe; the AV means the aromatic seed of Cuminum cyminum, a slender herb whose harvest Isaiah uses to teach the wisdom of God in husbandry. The plowman does not plow forever; in due season the husbandman doth “cast abroad the fitches, and scatter the cummin, and cast in the principal wheat and the appointed barley and the rie in their place” (Isa 28:25). And he threshes each seed by its own measure: “the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument, neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin; but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod” (Isa 28:27). A cart-wheel would crush so tender a seed; a light rod loosens it whole. So the LORD deals tenderly with tender things and hardly with hard, and “this also cometh forth from the LORD of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel.” The same cummin appears in Christ’s woe: “ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law” (Mat 23:23). Thus one little seed teaches two lessons: the exactness of God’s providence in the field, and the folly of exactness in tithes without justice in the heart.
webster_summary: A slender aromatic seed-herb, tithed by the Pharisee and beaten out with a rod, not crushed by the cart-wheel.

corruption_summary: No modern redefinition — only that we have half-forgotten the plant; the lesson is Isaiah’s, that the God who measures the threshing of cummin measures also the afflictions of His people.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no culture-war over cummin. If the word misleads at all it is only by unfamiliarity: the modern kitchen knows cumin as a curry-spice and forgets that it grew in the fields of Judah as a tithed crop. The one thing a reader must not do is despise it as a trifle, for the Holy Ghost has hung a great doctrine on this little seed. Isaiah asks whether the farmer, taught of God, threshes the tender cummin with the same heavy instrument he uses on the grain, and answers no: the cummin is beaten with a rod.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the measured providence of God. “The fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod” — and this, Isaiah says, “cometh forth from the LORD of hosts, which is wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working.” The husbandman does not crush the fragile seed under the cart-wheel that fits the wheat; he suits the stroke to the thing. So does the LORD with His people. He will not break the bruised reed, nor thresh the weak believer as He threshes the proud. Every affliction is measured to the frame that bears it, for our God is too wise to mistake His rod for His flail.

etymology: “Rue” the herb comes through Latin ruta from Greek rhyte, a strong-smelling shrub of the garden. It is unrelated to the English verb “to rue” (to regret), which is of Old English stock — a false friend within the language itself.
biblical_def: In the KJV rue is a bitter garden herb, named once, in Luke’s version of the woe our Lord pronounced on the Pharisees. Where Matthew has “mint and anise and cummin,” Luke writes, “woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judgment and the love of God” (Luk 11:42). The modern ear, hearing “rue,” thinks first of the verb — to rue, to regret, to be sorry — and may read a note of penitence where none is meant. But the rue of Luke is a plant: Ruta graveolens, a small evergreen shrub of bitter, pungent leaf, common in the gardens of the East. It is another of the trifling potherbs that the scrupulous Pharisee weighed out for the tithe. Luke names it, as Matthew names anise, to show how minute their exactness was and how vast their neglect: they measured the leaves of a bitter shrub and “passed over judgment and the love of God.” The remedy is Samuel’s ancient word, that outward exactness never purchases inward obedience: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). The law had indeed said, “Thou shalt truly tithe all the increase of thy seed” (Deu 14:22); but the tithe was meant to flow from a heart that loved God, not to be a bribe offered in the place of that love.
webster_summary: A bitter garden shrub tithed by the Pharisee — the herb, not the English verb of regret.
webster_full: RUE, a bitter, strong-scented garden shrub (Ruta graveolens); in the KJV a tithed potherb.

It stands for scruple in trifles joined to neglect of judgment and the love of God.

And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
corruption_summary: No modern ideology touches rue; the only trap is the pun — the herb is not the verb, and the sin in view is presumption, not penitence.
corruption_paragraphs: The pitfall in this word is a pun. English has two words spelled “rue”: the herb, from Latin ruta, and the old verb meaning to regret or repent, from Anglo-Saxon hreowan. They are wholly unrelated, and only chance has made them twins. A reader who hears the verb in Luk 11:42 may fancy the Pharisees were tithing their sorrow or their repentance, which turns the sense upside down. They were tithing a bitter shrub of their gardens — a thing so small that to weigh it out was the very picture of their strained and swallowed religion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no exactness in the outward can stand in the room of the inward. The Pharisee tithed his rue and passed over “the love of God” — and it is a solemn thing that the very love which is the sum of the law was the thing he left out. The fallen heart is ever willing to be busy and precise in what is cheap, that it may be spared the one duty that costs everything: to love God with all the heart. Rue teaches us to fear a religion of leaves without roots.

etymology: “Fitches” is an old plural (a form of “vetches”), which the KJV uses to render two different Hebrew words: qetsach in Isaiah, the black cummin or nutmeg-flower (Nigella sativa); and kussemeth in Ezekiel, a bread-grain, spelt akin to rye. One English word covers two plants.
biblical_def: In the KJV “fitches” is a farmer’s word, and it covers two different plants, for the translators used one homely English name for two Hebrew words. In Isaiah the fitches are a small black seed-spice, the qetsach or nutmeg-flower (Nigella sativa), sown and threshed beside the cummin: the husbandman doth “cast abroad the fitches, and scatter the cummin” (Isa 28:25), and “the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument... but the fitches are beaten out with a staff” (Isa 28:27). Here fitches stand, with cummin, for the tender seeds that God’s wise husbandry beats out gently and does not crush. In Ezekiel the same English word renders a wholly different thing — kussemeth, a bread-grain (spelt, akin to rye) — one of the seven poor stuffs the prophet was to mix in his siege-bread: “Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof” (Eze 4:9). That famine-loaf, baked of every scraping the city had left, was a sign of the straitness of the siege, when men would eat what beasts are fed. So the one word looks two ways: in Isaiah a spice of the garden, teaching the gentleness of providence; in Ezekiel a coarse grain of the famine, preaching the severity of judgment. The reader must let the context tell him which plant the AV means.

corruption_paragraphs: The difficulty here is not ideology but antiquity. “Fitches” is a form of “vetches,” an old word for a leguminous field-plant, and the translators pressed it into service for two unrelated Hebrew words. The modern reader, who never says “fitches” at all, is apt to think it one thing and miss that Isaiah’s fitch is a spice and Ezekiel’s a grain. Let context rule: where the seed is scattered with cummin and beaten with a staff, it is the black nutmeg-flower; where it is ground into siege-bread with wheat and barley and beans, it is spelt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the two hands of God’s providence. In Isaiah the fitch teaches His gentleness: the tender seed is not crushed under the wheel but loosened with a light staff, and this “cometh forth from the LORD of hosts.” In Ezekiel the same word teaches His severity: the coarse fitch goes into the bread of famine, the loaf of a besieged and rebellious city. The one God is the God of both fields — the garden where He deals tenderly and the beleaguered city where He deals justly — and the same hand that spares the cummin bakes the bread of siege.

etymology: “Rie” is the old spelling of rye, the grain Secale cereale, from Old English ryge. The Authorized Version keeps the older form; the same grain is meant.
biblical_def: In the KJV “rie” is simply rye, the hardy bread-grain, spelled after the older fashion. The word gives the modern reader no trouble of meaning, only of spelling; yet the two places it stands are worth marking, for both set rye among the ordinary providences of God in the field. The first is in the plagues of Egypt. When the hail smote the land it broke the flax and the barley, “but the wheat and the rie were not smitten: for they were not grown up” (Exo 9:32). The later grains, still tender in the blade, were spared — a small mercy woven into a great judgment, and a token that even in wrath the LORD remembers the harvest of the coming year. The second is in Isaiah’s parable of the husbandman, where rye is one of the appointed crops the wise farmer sows each in its place: he casts in “the principal wheat and the appointed barley and the rie in their place” (Isa 28:25). Every grain has its season and its ground, assigned by the God who taught the plowman his craft. The coarse rye of Ezekiel’s siege-loaf — if the “fitches” of Eze 4:9 be spelt, a near kinsman of rye — shows the other side: the same humble grain that feeds a nation in peace becomes the bread of a besieged city in judgment. Rye asks nothing of the reader but that he see God’s hand in the commonest crop of the field.
webster_summary: The old spelling of rye, a hardy bread-grain, twice set among the field-providences of God.

corruption_summary: No corruption at all — only an old spelling; the lesson is to see the LORD’s providence in the plainest grain of the field.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in the sense of this word, only in the spelling. “Rie” is rye, and the reader loses nothing by the older letters. If anything is easy to miss, it is the quiet mercy tucked into Exo 9:32: when the hail destroyed the flax and barley that were in the ear, the wheat and the rie escaped because they were later grains, still in the blade. The judgment was real, but it was not total; the God who sent the hail measured even its reach.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over the common field. Rye is no glamorous crop; it is the poor man’s grain, hardy in cold and thin soil. Yet Scripture names it twice, and both times to teach that the LORD orders the harvest: He spares the ungrown rie in the storm, and He appoints its place in the sown field. The Christian who learns to see God in his rye — in the plainest bread on the plainest table — will not fail to see Him in greater things. “This also cometh forth from the LORD of hosts.”

etymology: “Millet” comes through Old French from Latin milium, a small-grained cereal grass (Panicum miliaceum). The name marks its many tiny seeds — from mille, a thousand.
biblical_def: In the KJV millet is a small grain, named but once, among the poor stuffs of Ezekiel’s siege-bread. The word is not archaic in sense — millet is still millet — but the modern reader, who thinks of it as birdseed or a health-food curiosity, must be told what it meant on that prophet’s table. When Ezekiel was made a sign of the coming siege of Jerusalem, the LORD commanded him: “Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley, and beans, and lentiles, and millet, and fitches, and put them in one vessel, and make thee bread thereof” (Eze 4:9). No householder in plenty bakes bread of six grains and pulses swept together; that is famine-bread, the loaf of a city where the wheat is nearly gone and every last scraping must go into the pot. Millet, a coarse and humble grain, belonged to such a loaf. Behind the sign lies the sentence pronounced in Eden: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19). Bread is never far from the curse and the toil of a fallen world, and in judgment it grows dear indeed: “We gat our bread with the peril of our lives because of the sword of the wilderness” (Lam 5:9). Yet even under judgment the ordinance of labour holds — “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — and the humble millet of the siege-loaf preaches that daily bread, coarse or fine, is the gift of God to be received with thanks and earned with toil.
webster_summary: A small coarse cereal grain, named once, in the famine-bread of Ezekiel’s siege.

corruption_summary: No modern quarrel — only that we have forgotten millet was bread; and it preaches the doctrine of daily bread in a fallen and judged world.
corruption_paragraphs: Millet needs no rescue from a false modern sense; it needs only to be seen for what it was — food. To us it is fodder, or a fashionable grain in a bag from the health-shop; to the besieged of Jerusalem it was one of the last things left to bake. The whole force of Eze 4:9 hangs on the poverty of the mixture: wheat and barley are honest bread-corns, but beans, lentiles, millet, and fitches thrown into one vessel are the diet of desperation, weighed out by measure and eaten by measure, as the next verses show.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of daily bread. From Eden the sentence stood, “in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread”; and where men rebel, the LORD can make that bread scarce and dear, till a city bakes its millet by weight and eats it in fear. Let the well-fed Christian read Ezekiel’s loaf and repent of a careless heart. Every meal is mercy; the coarse grain no less than the fine is “our daily bread,” asked of the Father and earned by the sweat He appointed.

etymology: “Lentiles” (now spelt lentils) are the seeds of a pulse of the East (Lens culinaris), from Latin lens, lentis. The Authorized Version keeps the older spelling; the pottage of Genesis was red, and gave Edom (“red”) his name.
biblical_def: In the KJV lentiles are a common pulse, the small lens-shaped bean of the East, boiled into a thick red pottage. The word is only old in spelling; the thing is the lentil still. But one meal of lentiles has become a byword for the worst bargain ever struck. Esau came in from the field faint, and Jacob had pottage of lentiles: “then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright” (Gen 25:34). For a bowl of red stew a man sold the covenant birthright, the double portion, the line of promise — and the Holy Ghost sets him up forever as a warning against every “profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16). That is the profane heart in a single dish: it feels the present appetite and cannot feel the eternal weight, and so it trades the unseen inheritance for a thing that fills the belly and is gone. Yet lentiles are not evil; they are honest food. They were among the provisions brought to David in his flight (2Sa 17:28), and a field of them was the ground Shammah defended alone when “the people fled from the Philistines” (2Sa 23:11). The same humble pulse that fed the faithful ruined the profane — not by any fault in the food, but by the folly of a man who valued his soup above his soul.
webster_summary: A common red pulse — honest food, yet the price of Esau’s despised birthright.

corruption_summary: The food is honest; the sin is Esau’s — the profane heart that trades an eternal birthright for a present bowl.
corruption_paragraphs: The peril of this word is not a shift of meaning but a picture of the human heart, and it is as modern as this morning. Esau is the profane man — not the blasphemer, but the man to whom nothing is holy, who reckons the unseen and eternal as worth less than a warm meal now. Our age has raised his bargain into a creed: live for the present, seize the appetite, let tomorrow and the world to come look to themselves. Every soul that sells its Sabbath, its purity, its inheritance in Christ for a passing pleasure is doing Esau’s deed over a fresh bowl of lentiles.

The lentiles themselves are guiltless — good food, brought to David in the wilderness and defended by Shammah in the field. The evil was in Esau, who “despised his birthright.” Here is no honest language-drift to note away but a standing warning to be pressed home: weigh what you are asked to take against what you are asked to give up. The birthright was invisible, future, and infinite; the pottage was hot, present, and gone by evening. Reader, do not be a “profane person, as Esau.” Count the cost, and never let the belly of an hour buy away the blessing of eternity.

etymology: “Wafer” comes through Old French waufre from a Germanic root (kin to waffle and weave), naming a thin cake baked on a flat iron. In the KJV it renders Hebrew raqiq, a thin unleavened cake of the offerings.
biblical_def: In the KJV a wafer is a thin flat cake of unleavened bread, used in the holy offerings and likened to the manna. The modern reader hears “wafer” and may think of a communion-host of the Roman altar, or a light biscuit; the AV means a plain, thin, leaven-free cake, Hebrew raqiq, baked without yeast for the service of God. It stands among the priestly breads. At the consecration of Aaron the LORD commanded “unleavened bread, and cakes unleavened tempered with oil, and wafers unleavened anointed with oil: of wheaten flour shalt thou make them” (Exo 29:2); and Moses took from the basket “one unleavened cake, and a cake of oiled bread, and one wafer” and laid them on the fat of the offering (Lev 8:26). At the close of the Nazarite’s vow the priest took “one unleavened wafer” and put it upon his hands (Num 6:19). The wafer, then, is a bread of dedication, thin and pure, anointed with oil — a fit figure of a life offered wholly to God. And when Israel first gathered the manna, that bread from heaven, they found its taste “like wafers made with honey” (Exo 16:31): the daily gift of God as sweet as the holy cake of His altar. The reader should see in the wafer no wafer-god, but a simple, sincere, unleavened bread of offering.
webster_summary: A thin unleavened cake of the offerings, likened to the manna — not the wafer-host of Rome.

corruption_summary: Not a live postmodern redefinition but a caution: the KJV wafer is a bread of offering, not the consecrated host of the Roman Mass.
corruption_paragraphs: The word “wafer” now carries an association the KJV never intended: to many ears it means the round wafer of the Roman Mass, held to be transubstantiated into the body of Christ. The Authorized Version’s wafer is nothing of the kind. It is a thin unleavened cake of the Levitical offerings, a piece of ordinary wheaten dough baked without yeast and anointed with oil. A reader who imports the Mass into Exo 29:2 or Num 6:19 reads his own age’s error back into Moses.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the meaning of the unleavened wafer itself: a bread of dedication, thin, pure, and free of the leaven that puffs and sours. Such cakes were laid on the altar at the making of a priest and set in the hand of the Nazarite whose vow was fulfilled — tokens of a life set apart and offered whole to God, without the leaven of corruption. And the manna, God’s own bread from heaven, tasted like wafers made with honey: His daily provision as pure and sweet as the bread of His sanctuary. Let the wafer preach dedication and sincerity, not a wafer to be adored.

etymology: “Unleavened” is bread made without leaven — without the fermenting yeast or sour dough that makes bread rise. From the negative un- and leaven (Old French levain, Latin levare, to raise). The Hebrew is matstsah.
biblical_def: In the KJV unleavened bread is bread baked without leaven — without the yeast or sour dough that ferments the lump and makes it rise. The word itself is plain enough, but its weight is easily missed, for in Scripture unleavened bread is never merely a recipe; it is a sign. It is the bread of haste: on the night of the Passover Israel ate the lamb “roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it” (Exo 12:8), for they must eat and go, with no time to let the dough rise. It is the bread of the feast that followed: “Unleavened bread shall be eaten seven days; and there shall no leavened bread be seen with thee” (Exo 13:7), leaven being purged from every house. It is the bread of affliction: “seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, even the bread of affliction; for thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt in haste” (Deu 16:3), a bread to make Israel remember her low estate and her swift deliverance. And it is, at last, the bread of sincerity. Leaven in Scripture pictures the spreading, souring corruption of sin; so the Apostle turns the feast into a gospel: “Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” (1Co 5:7). The unleavened loaf preaches a purged and honest heart.
webster_summary: Bread without leaven — the sign of haste, affliction, and sincerity, purged of the corruption that leaven pictures.

Deu 16:3

Thou shalt eat no leavened bread with it; seven days shalt thou eat unleavened bread therewith, even the bread of affliction; for thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt in haste: that thou mayest remember the day when thou camest forth out of the land of Egypt all the days of thy life.
corruption_summary: The word keeps its meaning, but its lesson is live: leaven is the spreading corruption of sin, and the feast calls for a lump purged of malice and hypocrisy.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the danger is not that the word has changed but that its doctrine is forgotten. Unleavened bread still means bread without yeast; what the modern reader misses is that the whole Feast of Unleavened Bread was a seven-day sermon against sin. Leaven works secretly, spreads through the whole lump, sours and puffs it up — a perfect figure of corruption, which is why our Lord warned of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod. The command to sweep every crumb of leaven from the house was a command to hate the least remaining sin.

The Apostle presses it on the church as a live and searching thing: “let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1Co 5:8). This is no antiquarian note but a summons to holiness. Christ our Passover is slain; therefore the old leaven — malice, wickedness, hypocrisy, every secret sin that spreads and sours — must be purged out, that the church may be a new lump. The world calls such a life narrow; Scripture calls it unleavened. Keep the feast in sincerity and truth, for a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.

etymology: “Cracknels” are hard, dry, brittle cakes or biscuits — so called from the crackling sound they make; from Old French craquelin and English crack. They kept long, being dry.
biblical_def: In the KJV cracknels are hard, dry, brittle cakes — a plain, long-keeping biscuit, named from the crackling snap they give when broken. The word has all but vanished from modern speech, and the reader meets it only once, in a strange and sorrowful errand. Jeroboam’s child lay sick, and the king sent his wife in disguise to the old prophet Ahijah at Shiloh to learn the child’s fate: “take with thee ten loaves, and cracknels, and a cruse of honey, and go to him” (1Ki 14:3). The gift is a poor countrywoman’s present — common loaves, dry cracknels, a little honey — part of the disguise, for a queen bearing such fare would not be known. Yet no disguise deceives the blind prophet or the God who sent him; Ahijah met her at the door with heavy tidings before she spoke. The dryness of the cracknel is its whole nature: like the “dry and mouldy” bread the Gibeonites carried to feign a long journey (Jos 9:5), and the bread they “took hot” that was now “dry, and it is mouldy” by the time they came (Jos 9:12), the hard biscuit is travellers’ fare, baked to last. So even this forgotten word has its lesson: man packs his dry cracknels and lays his disguises, but the LORD is not mocked, and reads the heart beneath the veil.
webster_summary: Hard, dry, brittle biscuits that keep long — travellers’ fare, and part of a disguised queen’s gift.

corruption_summary: No modern redefinition, only a lost word; the lesson is that dry disguises cannot hide the heart from God.
corruption_paragraphs: “Cracknels” is simply an old word gone out of use, and there is no ideology to answer, only a picture to restore. A cracknel is a hard dry biscuit, the sort of bread that keeps because it holds no moisture to spoil — humble, cheap, and lasting. It belonged in the bundle of a plain country wife, which is exactly why Jeroboam chose it for his queen’s disguise: royalty does not carry cracknels. The dryness that makes the biscuit is the same dryness that makes the Gibeonites’ mouldy loaves a false witness of a long, hard road.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no disguise deceives the LORD. Jeroboam dressed his wife as a commoner and filled her hands with cracknels and honey, but the aged prophet, though his eyes were set with age, knew her step upon the threshold and met her with the word of God: “Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another?” So it is with every dry disguise the fallen heart contrives. Men pack their cracknels and change their garments to seem what they are not, but He who searches the reins reads the heart beneath the veil, and will not be mocked.
